name: Mailbird
tagline: Build a Windows email client with unified inbox, local search, and simple integrations

pricing.notes: Typical Standard subscription rate; lifetime options can also exist.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: 1 user, 1 email account and 1 device per license; knowledge-base support only.

tiers.name: Premium Yearly
tiers.limits: 1 user; unlimited email accounts; up to 3 devices; unlimited email tracking.
tiers.notes: Current promoted annual rate is $4.03/user/month paid yearly (about $48.36/year); the page shows a struck-through $5.75/month rate.

tiers.name: Premium Pay Once
tiers.limits: 1 user; unlimited email accounts; up to 3 devices; unlimited email tracking; 1 additional Premium license included in the current promotion.
tiers.notes: Current one-time promotional price is $99.75/user (page shows $399 regular); future major versions/features are not included unless the Lifetime Updates add-on is purchased.

pricing.freeTierCaps: 1 email account, 1 user and 1 device; knowledge-base support only
pricing.billingTerms: free + annual subscription + one-time license; no monthly subscription shown; 14-day money-back guarantee
pricing.hiddenCosts: The Pay Once offer excludes future major versions/features unless Lifetime Updates is added for $69; the optional Leave Me Alone bundle is $59. Promotional prices are dynamic. Multi-license discounts run from 5% for 2-10 licenses to 25% for 101+.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Mailbird, build a Windows email client with unified inbox, local search, and simple integrations. The hard boundary is windows polish, provider compatibility, app integrations, sync, and support, plus mail infrastructure, integrations, and client polish.
coreLoopDIY: Connect existing mailboxes to a Windows email client, index messages locally for fast search, provide a unified focused inbox, and send through each account's normal SMTP service.
whatYouLose: Windows polish, provider compatibility, app integrations, sync, and support
moatNotes: mail infrastructure, integrations, and client polish
ongoingBurden: IMAP quirks, OAuth, MIME, threading, search, attachments, offline sync, notifications, secure storage, and provider changes
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Mailbird because an email client can be rebuilt; operating a trusted mail service with excellent deliverability cannot. The recurring cost buys IMAP quirks, OAuth, MIME, threading, search, attachments, offline sync, notifications, secure storage, and provider changes, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: mailcow
priorArt.desc: Popular open-source mail-server suite that demonstrates the operational complexity of hosted mail.

alternatives.name: BlueMail Personal
alternatives.desc: A free Windows unified inbox with unlimited accounts, search and clusters; integrations are thinner.

facts.install: Install the Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android, or ChromeOS client and add existing mail accounts
facts.engines: Optional paid GemAI features use third-party large-language-model providers; the free Personal tier's core mail client does not require them
facts.dataFormat: Mail remains at the provider and is cached locally; BlueMail services may momentarily process data for push, spam protection, and optional GemAI, while some cross-device features store encrypted metadata
facts.gapVsPaid: BlueMail covers the unified inbox but has a much thinner ecosystem of embedded productivity apps and integrations than Mailbird.

alternatives.name: Edison Mail
alternatives.desc: Unified accounts, search and rules on Windows for free; integrations are not the point.

facts.install: Install the desktop or mobile app and add existing email accounts
facts.engines: Edison’s proprietary AI-based Assistant/search and smart-folder system; the model or backend is not disclosed on the checked official pages
facts.dataFormat: Messages remain with the mailbox provider and are cached in the client; Edison also processes account and message-derived data through its services, with separate controls for optional commerce-research participation
facts.gapVsPaid: Edison provides a unified inbox and search but does not reproduce Mailbird’s side-panel app and productivity-integration ecosystem.

alternatives.name: Mailspring
alternatives.desc: A modern open-source unified inbox for Windows; several workflow niceties remain Pro.

facts.install: Install the packaged desktop app for macOS, Windows, or Linux and create a Mailspring ID
facts.dataFormat: Mail is synchronized and indexed into a local database and cache; Mailspring's service stores account and feature metadata but says it does not store message content except for features such as shared threads
facts.gapVsPaid: Mailspring lacks Mailbird’s broad embedded-app integration layer, and several workflow conveniences remain paid.
facts.setupBlocker: A Mailspring ID is mandatory, and there are no mobile clients

alternatives.name: Spark Free
alternatives.desc: A polished Windows inbox with smart sorting and search; the ecosystem of side-panel apps is gone.

facts.install: Install Spark on macOS, Windows, iOS, or Android, create a Spark account, and connect existing mailboxes
facts.engines: Optional Spark +AI and AI Assistant features use third-party large-language-model providers; the ordinary free mail client does not require AI
facts.dataFormat: Mail remains at the provider and is indexed locally; encrypted synchronization and notification metadata, and temporarily queued send-later messages, can live on Spark's servers; AI excerpts may be sent to a disclosed provider when AI is used
facts.gapVsPaid: Spark is polished on Windows but does not offer Mailbird’s broad collection of side-panel productivity integrations.
facts.setupBlocker: Requires a Spark account and mailbox OAuth or credentials, but no server administration

alternatives.name: Thunderbird
alternatives.desc: The sturdy Windows answer with extensions and local search; visual polish varies by decade.

facts.install: Install the official Windows, macOS, or Linux package and add existing mail accounts
facts.dataFormat: Accounts, settings, indexes, address books, and locally downloaded messages live in the Thunderbird profile; message stores use mbox by default, with Maildir available, while IMAP originals remain at the provider
facts.gapVsPaid: Thunderbird’s extensions are powerful but less consistently integrated and polished than Mailbird’s built-in app ecosystem.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Wino Mail
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Open-source code, but the free Store build sells unlimited accounts; an account-capped unified inbox misses the job.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Standard plan and a personal desktop mail client DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Mailbird in an empty repository.
Use Tauri 2, React, TypeScript, SQLite, IMAP, SMTP, and OAuth where available; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: connect existing mailboxes to a Windows email client, index messages locally for fast search, provide a unified focused inbox, and send through each account's normal SMTP service.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Support one IMAP and SMTP account with credentials stored only in the OS keychain.
Index headers and message bodies locally with resumable sync and a visible status page.
Implement standards-based threading, folders, labels, archive, snooze, drafts, and search.
Render HTML email in a locked-down sandbox and block remote images by default.
Send multipart messages with attachments and preserve a local copy of every draft.
Add export, local cache reset, account reconnect, diagnostics, and safe logging.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out running a public mail server.
Deliberately leave out shared team inboxes and sales workflows.
Deliberately leave out mobile push services and provider-scale spam filtering.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
